metadata.file_name: Mathematics anxiety and self-efficacy as predictors of mathematics literacy.pdf
metadata.title: Mathematics anxiety and self-efficacy as predictors of mathematics literacy
metadata.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL EDUCATION IN SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used PISA 2003 and PISA 2012 student microdata for Greece, restricting to 15-year-old students enrolled in the PISA mathematics literacy focus strands. The authors report that computations were performed in SPSS with appropriate sampling weights, consistent with PISA’s complex random sampling design (students nested in schools). They did not report the specific weight variable name in the provided text, so the exact variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) cannot be extracted. For missing data, they imputed missing values (see missing_data_handling) before estimating regression models; no replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Greece PISA 2003 and PISA 2012 mathematics literacy samples (mathematics literacy as the focus domain in both survey years). Included students with available data after handling missingness via imputation; the paper states that missingness on variables of interest was imputed because no individual variable exceeded 20% missingness. The analytic sample comprises 4627 students from 2003 and 5125 students from 2012, spanning Grades 7–11 (with Grade 11 as the reference category in regression).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two OLS regression models: Model 1 (demographics only) R² = 20.4%; Model 2 (adds anxiety, self-efficacy, and interaction) R² = 34.1%. Effect sizes reported via partial η²; coefficients in Table 3 show: ESCS B=24.14 (p<.001), Anxiety B=-20.46 (p<.001), Self-efficacy B=26.94 (p<.001), Interaction (Anxiety×Self-efficacy) B=-3.66 (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2003 & 2012 Greece mathematics literacy the study leveraged socioeconomic status, mathematics self-efficacy, mathematics anxiety, and their interaction (plus grade and survey year) to predict mathematics literacy, finding that the full model explained 34.1% of the variance and that socioeconomic status was the most potent predictor while anxiety and self-efficacy had significant opposite-direction associations. This indicates that mathematics performance interventions in Greece should prioritize reducing mathematics anxiety and strengthening mathematics self-efficacy, while also addressing socioeconomic disparities that remain the strongest driver of literacy differences, though the non-experimental design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed two nationally representative Greek samples from PISA 2003 and PISA 2012, focusing on mathematics literacy for 15-year-olds. Mathematics literacy was treated as a PV-based achievement score (five plausible values), and the authors followed the single-PV approach by conducting analyses with one plausible value at random. They estimated two OLS multiple regression models: Model 1 with demographic controls (R² = 20.4%) and Model 2 adding mathematics anxiety, mathematics self-efficacy, and their interaction (R² = 34.1%). In Model 2, mathematics self-efficacy was positively related to literacy (B=26.94, p<.001), mathematics anxiety was negatively related (B=-20.46, p<.001), and the Anxiety×Self-efficacy interaction was significant (B=-3.66, p<.001). The paper reports that computations used appropriate sampling weights and imputes missing data via iterative Markov Chain Maximum Likelihood; however, the design is observational and the regression framework is not ML, so predictive performance should not be interpreted as causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper uses regression-based prediction (not machine learning algorithms), the schema requires ML technique fields; therefore ml_techniques.primary is left null and all_techniques is empty because no ML learners (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM) are reported. The study’s main results are regression coefficients and R² from OLS models, not ML model comparisons. This is an observational, model-based analysis rather than an empirical ML pipeline.
